167-american-hand-book-of-the-daguerreot:
S. D. Humphrey's handbook gave American photographers the approved methods of their art. The American Hand Book of the Daguerreotype, in its fifth edition of 1858, covers preparing chemicals and combinations for heliographic impressions. Daguerreotype, electrotype, and related processes all appear.

Humphrey writes for practitioners, with recipes, cautions, and workshop detail rather than theory. Page marks in this electronic text follow the print original. The book shows photography as a hands-on trade in its first decades. Collectors and historians still consult it for period practice. Humphrey's fifth edition shows a craft maturing from novelty into a steady trade.
19983-recollections-of-europe:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote Recollections of Europe from his years abroad, 1826 to 1833. He grants it may seem late to describe the ordinary traits of Europe's peoples. Most people, he notes, judge other nations through reports alone. No two witnesses report the same country in the same way. His own account is what the book offers. Cooper lived in England, France, Switzerland, and Italy in those years.

Cooper was America's first writer to win fame across the Atlantic. His European books mix travel, politics, and national comparison. He judges monarchies and republics with a democrat's bias. The Recollections preserve an American eye on Europe after Napoleon. They also show fame's burdens abroad. Historians read them beside his novels with profit.
20926-the-register-of-ratlinghope:
A prior and twenty-nine canons held Ratlinghope at the Dissolution, yet its past stays dim. The Register of Ratlinghope notes its goods were worth five pounds, eleven shillings yearly. In May 1546 they were sold to Robert Longe, a London mercer.

Parish registers keep births, weddings, and burials across long runs of years. Shropshire's Ratlinghope, a wild hill parish, speaks here in bare lists. Names and dates that look dry hold whole lost lives in seed. Family and local historians mine such registers for kin, tenure, and the slow change of a place through plague, war, and peace.
21006-the-governments-of-europe:
Working accounts of how Europe's states run fill Frederic Austin Ogg's The Governments of Europe. His 1913 book treats western and central Europe as the systems then stood. Each land's form, he aims to show, must be seen as it works in fact.

Cabinets, parliaments, kings, and courts pass in clear, school-ready order. Ogg, a noted teacher of government, wrote for students who needed facts fast. His survey froze Europe's old order one year before it crashed in war. Readers can still use it to grasp the world the Great War swept away in four hard years.
21114-heroes-of-modern-europe:
Alice Birkhead's Heroes of Modern Europe, first published in London in 1913, tells European history through lives. Early chapters cover Dante, Lorenzo the Magnificent, and Savonarola, the prior of San Marco. Martin Luther, Emperor Charles V, and William the Silent follow as the story moves north.

Birkhead wrote other popular histories, including lives of Marie Antoinette and Peter the Great. Eight illustrations support the text, which opens with the fall of Rome and the coming of Teutonic invaders. The book offers young readers a parade of poets, rulers, and reformers, each standing for a turn in Europe's story from the Middle Ages onward.
21188-tom-swift-and-his-giant-telescope:
Victor Appleton's Tom Swift returns in this 1939 volume, published by Whitman of Racine, Wisconsin. Tom tells his chum Ned Newton that his new device should teach him more about the planets. The giant telescope is the latest project from the Swift works at Shopton.

Suspicions, an accident, and a murderous attempt follow in the chapter list. Tom is drugged, goes deep-sea diving, and is trapped by a sea monster before success arrives. The ten-chapter telling is shorter and punchier than the older Tom Swift books. It shows the young inventor series still running on invention, danger, and loyal friends.
21539-the-blue-envelope:
Roy J. Snell's The Blue Envelope, a 1922 adventure story for girls, opens with a disappearance in a horseshoe bay. Two girls fish for shrimps between rocky cliffs, one rowing, one lifting a wire net. Marian, the elder, was raised on the Alaskan tundra.

Marian hunted rabbits, ptarmigan, caribou, and white wolves with her father in her teens. She shoots as steady and sure as most boys her age. Chapters promise a visit to the Chukches, a dread white line, and a lonesome island. The blue envelope itself vanishes mid-tale, and its secret drives the hunt to the end.
21704-six-months-at-the-cape:
Letters home make up this travel book by R. M. Ballantyne, written to a friend he calls Periwinkle. Ballantyne had spent six years as a young clerk for the Hudson's Bay Company in Canada. That trip taught him to look closely at new lands and write down what he saw. Here he turns the same sharp eye on South Africa, at the Cape.

The letters describe the country, its towns, its people, and the daily life of a visitor far from home. Ballantyne later became famous for boys' adventure tales like The Coral Island. This book shows the working traveler behind those tales, gathering facts on the spot because readers had caught errors in his early work.
886-letters-from-the-cape:
Lady Duff Gordon wrote these letters from the Cape of Good Hope, edited by John Purves for a 1921 edition. Ill and seeking a warmer climate, she travelled to South Africa and wrote home about the land, its peoples, and its ways, with the candour and wit that made her letters famous.

The letters mix travel, health, and social observation, describing farms, towns, and the mixed society of the Cape. Purves's foreword notes they are less familiar than her Egyptian letters, yet just as vivid. The book gives readers a Victorian lady's view of South Africa, sharp, humane, and free of cant.
american-hand-book-of-the-daguerreotype:
S. D. Humphrey wrote this practical manual on the daguerreotype, the first widely used form of photography. The title page of this fifth edition is dated New York, 1858, and promises the most approved and convenient methods for preparing the chemicals and combinations used in the art. Humphrey's preface says working photographers had long wanted one concise, reliable handbook.

The chapters give working recipes and procedures. They cover coating and polishing plates, mixing chemicals, using the camera, and developing the image. The related electrotype process and other ways of taking pictures by light are included too. It is a trade manual, not a history, written for portrait studios at the height of the daguerreotype trade. For modern readers it preserves the exact bench practice of early photography.
an-autobiography-of-anthony-trollope:
An Autobiography, by Anthony Trollope, tells the most successful English novelist of his age how he did it. Trollope's contents begin with his education from 1815 to 1834 and a chapter on his mother, the writer Frances Trollope. Then comes the General Post Office, which employed him from 1834, and Ireland, where his first two novels were written in the 1840s while he rode his postal rounds.

Success arrives chapter by chapter: Barchester Towers and The Three Clerks, Doctor Thorne, the Cornhill Magazine and Framley Parsonage, Orley Farm, The Small House at Allington. Trollope pauses for three famous chapters on novels and the art of writing them, on living English novelists, and on criticism itself. He counts his earnings, defends his daily page quota, and treats authorship as honest trade work. No Victorian writer left a plainer account of the business of books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agape:
Agape begins from funeral feasts honouring the dead, a practice reaching back almost to worship's beginnings. The dead beyond the tomb were thought to gain pleasure and advantage from offerings, which explains funeral furniture for their use. Arms, vessels, and clothes, not subject to decay, needed no renewal, but food did, hence feasts at set seasons. Yet the departed gained no relief from offerings to his shade unless accompanied by obligatory rites.

Nor was the funeral feast mere commemoration, since it was a true communion, with guests' food really meant for the departed. Milk and wine were poured on the earth around the tomb, while solid food passed through a hole in the tomb to the corpse. The practice was almost universal in the Graeco-Roman world. The entry then relates the agape to the Last Supper and the Eucharist, and cites Batiffol, Funk, Keating, and Leclercq.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-pop:
Alexander Pope was an English poet, born in London in May 1688 and dead at Twickenham in May 1744. Both his parents were Catholics, and he lived and died in the faith of his birth. His father, a linen merchant in Lombard Street, retired on a moderate fortune to Kensington, then Binfield, then Chiswick. He died there in 1717, after which Pope moved with his mother.

In November 1713 Pope issued proposals for a subscription translation of Homer's Iliad into English verse, the work that turned his fortunes. Later he fell deeply under the influence of Bolingbroke, and with the Dunciad of 1743 his literary activity ceased, though he tried to gather his works for an authoritative edition. No writer ever made more enemies, the entry says: Pope lashed Bufo, Sporus, Sappho, Atosa, and scores of others by name or thin disguise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antipope:
An antipope is a rival claimant to the Holy See, opposing a canonically elected pope. Unlawful pretenders recur through Church history, often exercising papal functions against the true holder. Hergenröther counts thirty.

Hippolytus, third century, Novatian in 251, Felix II in 355-365, Ursicinus in 366-367, Eulalius in 418-419, and Laurentius in 498-501. Constantine II in 767, Philip, eighth century, and Anastasius in 855. Leo VIII in 956-963, Boniface VII in 974, John XVI, tenth century, Gregory in 1012, and Sylvester III in 1044. Benedict X in 1058, Honorius II in 1061-72, and Guibert, or Clement III, in 1080-1100. Theodoric in 1100, Aleric in 1102, Maginulf in 1105, and Burdin, called Gregory VIII, in 1118. Anacletus II in 1130-38, Victor IV in 1159-64, Pascal III in 1164-68, Calixtus III in 1168-77, Innocent III in 1178-80, and Nicholas V in 1328-30. Robert of Geneva, Clement VII, 20 September 1378 to 16 September 1394, and Amadeus of Savoy, Felix V, November 1439 to April 1449. See also Dioscorus (died 530) and John XXIII (1370-1419), not the twentieth-century pope of that name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cope:
Herbert Thurston's entry defines the cope, Latin pluviale or cappa, as a long liturgical mantle, open in front and fastened at the breast with a band or clasp. Surviving monuments, pictures, and early copes alike show remarkably little change in the vestment from earliest ages. It differed from the earlier chasuble form only in this: the chasuble's straight edges were sewn together in front, the cope's left open.

The most conspicuous change over the past thousand years and more lies in hood shape, a feature in no way essential. History traces the earliest mention of a cappa to Gregory of Tours and the Miracula of Saint Martin. Meanwhile the old cappa nigra, or cappa choralis, a black choir cope, open or partly open in front and commonly hooded, continued in use. Under all these forms the cope has not substantially changed its character or shape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eastern-vicar:
In 1847 the Cape vicariate divided into Eastern and Western halves, and the Eastern half became its own vicariate. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how the Eastern vicariate was later cut three times more. As it stands, it runs from the Orange River in the north to the Indian Ocean in the south. It is bounded west by a chain of civil districts and east by Tembuland, Griqualand East, and Basutoland.

On 27 December 1847 Doctor Devereux was consecrated at Cape Town as bishop of Paneas and first vicar apostolic, by Doctor Griffith, under whom he had worked nine years. A gift through the Dhanis family of Belgium aided the new mission. The entry counts thirty-seven men religious and three hundred and thirty-one women religious, serving more than thirteen thousand Catholics, few of them natives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-europe:
Europe is treated here in a long survey article that moves from the land itself to the faith of its peoples. It opens with the name, traced to Aegean sailors who used Semitic words for sunset and sunrise for lands west and east of their sea. It then maps the continent's bounds, from North Cape to Cape Tarifa, and measures its length, breadth, and area. 

The second half turns to people and religion. It covers population, political divisions, and the spread of Christianity from its early centuries through the Crusades, the Reformation, and the Counter-Reformation. It closes with the present state of religion country by country, how each state treats its churches, and full tables of religious statistics drawn from censuses around 1900. The result is a snapshot of a continent on the eve of modern change.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-vi-an:
When Pope Sergius IV died in June 1012, a rival claimant known only as Gregory challenged the election of Benedict VIII and had himself made pope by a small faction. The entry follows this brief claimant from his hurried elevation to his swift expulsion from Rome.

Driven out, Gregory crossed to Germany and asked King Henry II for backing in December 1012. Henry promised a hearing under canon law and Roman custom, yet stripped him of the papal insignia and told him to stop acting as pope. After that rebuke, the record says, history hears nothing more of him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-viii-:
Mauritius Burdinus, a Frenchman born probably at Limoges, rose through Cluny and the Spanish church to become Archbishop of Braga before his career broke on imperial politics. Suspended by Paschal II after a quarrel with the primate, he went to Rome, won the pope's trust, and was sent to deal with Emperor Henry V in 1117.

On that mission Burdinus changed sides, crowned Henry at Easter, and was excommunicated. Months later Henry had a bribed Roman assembly proclaim him pope under the name Gregory, on 8 March 1118. Repeated excommunications followed, and Callistus II finally held him prisoner in monasteries until his death about 1137.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guadeloupe:
Basse-Terre's diocese gathers Guadeloupe with Les Saintes, Marie-Galante, La Désirade, and the French parts of St. Martin and St. Bartholomew in the West Indies. Columbus reached the main island in November 1493 and named it for Spain's Madonna of Guadalupe, and the island stayed French from 1653 apart from short English occupations.

After years under a prefect apostolic, reform of the colonial clergy led to a bull of September 1850 creating the bishopric as suffragan of Bordeaux. Its first bishop, the famed preacher Lacarrière, served from 1851 to 1853, and by 1905 the diocese counted 182,112 people, 37 parishes, and 54 priests beside its bishop and vicars-general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hope:
Hope, in its widest sense, is desire for something joined with expectation of obtaining it. Scholastics call it a movement of appetite toward a future good, hard to attain yet possible. This article limits itself to hope as a factor in the supernatural order, where it is defined as a divine virtue.

By that virtue, Christians confidently expect, with God's help, to reach eternal felicity and to have the means of securing it. Hope counts as divine not only because its object is God, but because of its special origin. It is an infused virtue, not the product of repeated acts or personal industry. Like faith and charity, God implants it directly in the soul, lifting a faculty beyond created limits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-sharpe:
James Sharpe, alias Pollard, born at York in 1577 and dead at Lincoln in 1630, was converted young and studied for priesthood at Valladolid's English College. Ordained in 1604, he returned to England in 1606. A singular trial awaited him there. Believing he must help his parents toward the faith, he visited them at Everingham. He was insidiously kept prisoner at home.

At home, disputations and entreaties alternated with threats, violence, and constant surveillance. His mother begged him on her knees to yield. His father asked authorities to keep him close at home in England rather than exile him. His constancy prevailed. Taken eventually to the archbishop's prison, then deported, he had entered the Society of Jesus in 1608 and became a noted missioner, constancy under family pressure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois:
Jean-François La Harpe, a French critic and poet born in Paris in 1739 and dead in 1803. He lost his father at ten, was raised by Sisters of Charity, and studied free at Collège d'Harcourt. Satirical verses landed him in Fort-l'Évêque prison, yet at twenty he published his Heroïdes and won fame with the tragedy Warwick.

La Harpe clung so close to Voltaire that wits called him Voltaire's monkey, though later tragedies failed. At the Mercure from 1768 he wrote notable criticism, won three Academy prizes in a row for praises of Henry IV, Fénelon, and Racine, and entered the Academy in 1776. His banned play Mélanie attacked religious vows and was widely read despite its tedium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-trappe: This 1913 reference piece on La Trappe — the Cistercian abbey. Edmond Obrecht unfolds its austere tale. The monks keep the silent rule. Normandy guards the holy house. The order bless its name. Its 1664 reform is famed. Its austere rule is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lippe: A 1913 entry on Lippe — the German principality. Hermann Sacher gives its storied past. Its princes ruled the Teutoburg land. The entry keeps its modest record. A state of the empire's west. Its 12th-century lords are famed. Its principality is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-aube: Philippe-Aubert de Gaspé wrote Les Anciens Canadiens, the beloved novel of old French Canada. This entry covers his career, his novel, and his fame. The storyteller of New France's twilight: his beloved first novel charmed readers in two languages alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protopope: The protopope is the Eastern archpriest first among the priests. This entry explains his office, his rights, and his history. The dean of the Byzantine clergy: his jeweled staff leads the parish priests in solemn procession each feast day in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ruspe: Ruspe was the see of St. Fulgentius in Africa. This brief entry notes its bishop, its site, and its early church history. A quiet name made great by a saint: its exiled bishop defied the Vandals in Sardinia's exile in the 500s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schaumburg-li: Schaumburg-Lippe became the principality of the Weser hills. This entry covers its princes, its Catholics, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Bückeburg land: its small churches serve the principality in the Weser's hills in the empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shrine-of-gua: The Shrine of Guadalupe is the basilica of Mexico's Virgin. This entry traces its apparition, its basilica, and its fame. The tilma of the Tepeyac hill: its dark image draws the millions in Mexico's capital in the basilica of the Virgin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sinope: Sinope, the Pontic city of the Black Sea, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Asia Minor: its old walls crown the sea in Pontus' shore in the Black Sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suppression-o: The suppressions were the fall of the European houses. This long entry examines their Joseph, their spoils, and their sorrow. The ruin of the old orders: their broad lands filled the princes in the 1780s' Josephinism in the empire of the Habsburgs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-pope: The Pope is the vicar of Christ. This very long entry examines his primacy, his infallibility, and his history. The shepherd of the universal flock: his ancient keys crowned Rome in the 100s of the martyrs in the old catacombs.

The chopper was VULCAN. The data were instrument. The scan was wavelength. The results were scan. The chopper was DOE's.
doe-osti-3008907-advanced-modeling-of-be: Smashing atoms on a budget got its DOE tune-up, and this text squeezes more from collider beams. The pages detail the beam physics. The accelerator crew gets its method. The tune-up was advanced modeling. The physics was beam.

The hydrogen folks get their specs. The duty was heavy. The specs were hydrogen. The considerations were design. The device was HyStEP.

The production was stable isotope. The data were nuclear. The methods were novel. The isotope was stable. The domestic was method.
doe-osti-3022995-final-design-for-therma: TEX got lithium-benchmarked, and this DOE final designs thermal experiments. The pages detail the absorber findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The validation was benchmarks. The data were nuclear. The TEX was design. The absorbers were lithium. The benchmarks were validation.
doe-osti-3367368-luminescence-properties: Europium got luminesced, and this DOE text dopes LiCaAlF6 sodium. The pages detail the properties findings. The physicists get their data. The doped was sodium co-doped. The data were physicist. The 6 were LiCaAlF. The europium were properties. The doped were europium.
doe-osti-3408696-electrochemical-testing: Oil operations produce wastewater laced with metals — and someone has to check what's in it. Carson and Kendall test electrochemical methods that use electric current to spot and measure those metals in petroleum wastewater. Faster, cheaper monitoring keeps pollution from slipping by unnoticed.
doe-osti-3409772-novel-method-for-domest: Isotopes got domestically-produced, and this DOE final covers stable isotope methods. The pages detail the novel findings. The nuclear folks get their closeout. The CRADA was 667. The closeout was nuclear. The production were isotope. The 667 were CRADA. The domestic were novel.
doe-osti-3427060-novel-three-in-one-high: DC cables got 3-in-1-superconducted, and this DOE text covers high-temperature grid cables. The pages detail the novel findings. The grid folks get their data. The revolution was grid. The data were grid. The superconducting were DC. The grid were revolution.
dope: Dope, Sax Rohmer's novel of London's drug underworld. The dope trade. This book preserves that thriller. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
govdocs-archive_org-OperationNorthwoodsU:
Tom Secker compiled Operation Northwoods: The Ultimate Collection as the fullest single gathering of the declassified papers on the 1962 proposals. Secker, who researches state secrecy, adds his own introduction. The documents concern both Northwoods and the CIA's paramilitary campaign against Castro's Cuba.

Memos, plans, and histories appear in sequence, letting readers trace how the false-flag proposals rose through the Joint Chiefs and died at the White House. The collection's use is completeness: the paper trail in one place, from the record itself. It stands as a researcher's dossier on the best-documented false-flag plan of the Cold War, documented in the government's own files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HandwritingExpe: nsia-HandwritingExperts Handwriting Experts: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-thern-mythology-vol-:
Benjamin Thorpe published Northern Mythology in 1851, gathering the popular traditions and superstitions of Scandinavia and North Germany into three volumes. Volume I includes the Grottasöngr, the old song of the magic mill that ground out gold and then war.

Thorpe collected tales, charms, and customs from the people who still told and practiced them, then set them beside the old myths they descended from. His method helped make folklore a field a reader could hold in one book. The work became a classic of folklore studies, and its first volume remains a rich store of northern legend, belief, and story for any student of the North.
letters-from-the-cape:
Lucie Duff Gordon's Letters from the Cape were reissued by Oxford University Press in 1921. An editor's foreword says they are less familiar than Lady Anne Barnard's letters. Their first life was brief and partly hidden.

The letters first appeared in Galton's Vacation Tourists, third series, in 1864. Their simplicity and candor won brief public esteem there. Then the miscellany was forgotten, and the letters sank with it. Duff Gordon writes of South Africa with the same open eye she brought to Egypt. This reissue rescued a sharp, kind travel record. Her South African stay came before the Egyptian years. The same independence of mind marks both famous letter collections.
letters-to-sir-william-windham-and-mr-po:
Henry St. John, Viscount Bolingbroke, wrote these letters to Windham and Pope. Cassell published the volume in London, Paris, and Melbourne in 1894. An introduction traces Bolingbroke's life from his birth in 1678.

He was born at the family manor of Battersea, then a country village. His grandfather Sir Walter lived there with Cromwell's chief justice's daughter. Bolingbroke rose to lead Queen Anne's government, then fled into exile. His letters mix politics, philosophy, and friendship with Pope. They preserve a brilliant, fallen statesman's private voice. Pope, the poet, was Bolingbroke's close friend and ally. Their letters mix verse talk with high political memory.
lives-of-the-english-poets-prior-congrev:
Cassell's 1891 volume prints Johnson on Prior, Congreve, Blackmore, and Pope. Johnson wrote these lives at age sixty-eight. His Life of Pope occupies the largest share here. An introduction retells Boswell pressing him about Prior's impure tales.

Johnson replied that nothing in Prior excites to lewdness. Prior, he insisted, is a lady's book for any library. He praised Congreve's wit while condemning his plays' morals. Blackmore's religious purpose raised Johnson's estimate of his Creation poem. Lord Hailes censured Prior's tales as an eternal opprobrium. Boswell urged the point before Johnson dismissed his questionings.
love-affairs-of-the-courts-of-europe:
Love Affairs of the Courts of Europe is a popular history by Thornton Hall. Hall was a barrister and a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries. His chapters roam the royal courts of Europe across past centuries. Titles promise a comedy queen, the Bonnie Prince's bride, and a peasant who won an empress.

Readers meet Richelieu the rake, the Sun King and a widow, and Bianca of Tuscany. A friend of Marie Antoinette appears, as do rival sisters and a mistress of intrigue. Hall tells these tales for pleasure, not for the classroom. Each chapter is a short, juicy court romance from real history. Together they show how love and power mixed at court.
medieval-europe:
H. W. C. Davis wrote Medieval Europe for the Home University Library. The book is number thirteen in that set for home study. Davis was a fellow and tutor at Balliol College, Oxford.

Chapters start with the fall of the Roman Empire. Barbarian kingdoms, feudal rule, and the papacy come next in order. Later heads treat the medieval state, the Crusades, and the free towns. Maps of the Frankish lands, France, and the Holy Roman Empire aid the text. A note on books at the end guides further study. Davis packs a thousand years into a short, clear survey.
memoir-of-father-vincent-de-paul-religio:
A. M. Pope turned the Memoir of Father Vincent de Paul into English. He was a monk of La Trappe, as the title states. Bishop Cameron of Arichat wrote the preface to this edition.

The preface praises virtue as the one true source of rank. It tells of his first ten years in America, now in English. A short sketch of his order, his life, and his house comes first. That sketch, the preface says, adds weight to his own plain tale. Even pagan voices, the preface says, praise such a marked life. Persecutors too can be forced to honor the folk they hurt.
nasa-tm-19660009115-loss-process-for-hel:
S J Bauer at Goddard wrote this December 1964 paper on how helium ions vanish from the upper atmosphere. Ions are charged atoms, made when sunlight strikes the thin upper air. Helium ions do not last forever there. Some process removes them, and its rate shapes the layer's makeup. Bauer names that loss process as his whole subject.

The upper air's mix of ions affects radio signals that pass through it. It also affects how satellites read the region with their instruments. A clear loss rate makes models of the ionosphere more honest. Bauer's short paper belongs to the careful work that turned scattered rocket and satellite readings into a coherent picture of the charged upper air.
nasa-tm-19690016179-the-global-structure:
L. H. Brace of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint, numbered X-621-69-158, on the global structure of ionosphere temperature. Satellite observations supply the electron temperatures mapped here, from the upper F region into the protonosphere above it. A worldwide temperature map shows how the charged upper air gains and loses its heat.

Observations are plotted pole to pole at one thousand kilometers, then sorted by local time. Separate sections treat solar cycle changes and the polar ionosphere at solar minimum, winter against summer. Higher up, the protonosphere's daily swing and its nightside pattern across latitudes are mapped. A closing discussion weighs the processes that control the temperature, latitude by latitude and hour by hour.
nasa-tm-19710002046-effect-of-interactin:
Martin Hersch and Louis A. Povinelli of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in November 1970. It studies how swirling air changes the path of a jet fired into a supersonic stream. Such mixing matters in engines that burn fuel in very fast air.

Helium was shot at sonic speed into three kinds of flow. One held a pair of counter-rotating vortices, one a single vortex, and one no vortex at all. Injectors with swept edges made the swirls. Downstream, the jet pushed deeper with the double-edge injector than with the single-edge one. The team also varied the injection pressure across the runs.
nasa-tm-19710029182-retention-and-applic:
W. David Brown and Nancy Milly wrote this report for Marshall's Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory. It was revised on September 14, 1971, and issued as NASA TM X-64574. As the Saturn rocket program wound down, NASA risked losing hard-won engineering lessons. The report addresses how to keep that experience and apply it to future programs.

Its bulk is organized as working indexes. A hardware index sorts lessons by equipment, from amplifiers, batteries, and cables to computers, connectors, and power supplies. A problem index sorts them by cause, covering design, human error, maintenance, manufacturing, and procedures. Condition indexes and graphs let engineers find past failures by symptom. Conclusions and recommendations up front state how the collected experience should be retained and reused.
nasa-tm-19720003184-the-solar-envelope:
F Burlaga of NASA wrote this October 1971 study, NASA TM X-65739, on the region he calls the solar envelope. The envelope spans from about two to twenty five solar radii out from the Sun. Inside it, the solar wind changes character as it streams outward. Burlaga asked how those changes shape the wind later measured near Earth. The report runs to about fifty pages.

Within the envelope, the wind speed passes two key thresholds. It becomes supersonic, then faster than magnetic waves can travel. Magnetic energy in the flow also evolves across this zone. By the time the wind reaches Earth's distance, those early changes are built in. The study links near Sun physics to spacecraft readings taken far away.
nasa-tm-19720016238-analytic-short-perio:
David Fisher wrote this NASA technical memorandum on analytic short-period lunar and solar perturbations of artificial satellites. The Moon and Sun tug satellites in small, quick, repeating patterns that orbit calculators must account for. Fisher's aim was a fast analytic theory, giving formulas rather than slow step-by-step computation.

He generalizes Kozai's short-period luni-solar theory so it works for any tilt of the ecliptic and any tilt of the Moon's orbit. Analytic first-order lunar perturbations to the orbital elements are derived in the analysis. A worked section applies the theory to the semi-major axis of the Intelsat 3F3 satellite. Results and conclusions close the paper, with two appendices carrying supporting derivations.
our-hundred-days-in-europe: Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote Our Hundred Days in Europe about a summer excursion in his late seventies. His daughter Amelia traveled with him, and the book is dedicated to her. The hosted sample shows the dedication and contents only. The contents trace the route: Liverpool, Chester, London, and Windsor. Cambridge, Oxford, York, and Edinburgh follow. Then come Stratford, Bath, and Stonehenge, and finally Paris. No narrative page appears in the sample.
peaceless-europe:
Francesco Saverio Nitti, who had been prime minister of Italy, published Peaceless Europe in 1922. His opening chapter asks who still remembers Europe in the first months of 1914. Some thirty million dead, he writes, have dug a chasm between two ages, and famine reaped hardest of all.

The chapters attack the peace treaties as a continuation of the war by other means. Nitti prints secret documents from the Peace Conference, including a long unpublished letter from Lloyd George. The book argues that a vindictive settlement leaves victors anxious and Europe without real peace.
podcast-joerogan-yA3Edy95BPE:
Joe Rogan questions former CIA officer Mike Baker about UFOs in this clip from the Joe Rogan Experience. Baker, a frequent guest, usually talks spies and world affairs. Here Rogan turns him to the question fans always ask: what does Langley really know?

Baker gives the agency-style answer, careful about what can be said and what is guesswork. He discusses how intelligence services would handle unknown craft as a threat question first. Rogan pushes for what Baker personally believes after years inside. The clip is short but telling, a spymaster's measured take on the phenomenon.
skookum-chuck-fables-bits-of-history-thr: Skookum Chuck Fables, with the sub-title Bits of History, Through the Microscope, rests on a Canada copyright of 1915 held by R. D. Cumming. Some pieces had first come out in the Ashcroft Journal. The contents list fables of the Rolling Stone, Cultus Johnny, the Booby Man, and Hard Times Hance. Later tales treat the Too Sure Man, the Unloved Man, Simple Simon up to date, the High Class Eskimo, and the Real Santa Claus.
the-doctrine-of-evolution-its-basis-and-: Henry Edward Crampton, professor of zoology at Columbia, gave the Hewitt lectures of 1906-1907 as The Doctrine of Evolution. This printing, from Columbia University Press in 1916, notes a first issue in 1911 and reprints since. Only the front matter is present here. None of the lectures' text appears, beyond the title pages that name their scope: the basis and reach of evolution.
the-gourmet-s-guide-to-europe: Lieutenant-Colonel Newnham-Davis and Algernon Bastard wrote The Gourmet's Guide to Europe. Newnham-Davis also edited the volume. Grant Richards printed it in London in 1903. Only front matter is present here. It gives a publisher's announcement and the title page. The announcement covers companion books on where and how to dine in London and in Paris. No dining entries, menus, or town-by-town advice are present. The guide's own picks and judgments cannot be told from what is here.
the-hairy-ape:
Eugene O'Neill wrote The Hairy Ape, subtitled a comedy of ancient and modern life in eight scenes. The cast list names Robert Smith, called Yank, plus Paddy, Long, Mildred Douglas, her aunt, a second engineer, a guard, and a group of stokers. Scene one sits in the stokers' sleeping quarters of an ocean liner just out of New York.

Stage directions shape the opening in detail. Narrow steel bunks stand three deep, the ceiling presses low, and the men shout, curse, laugh, and sing while bottles pass from hand to hand. O'Neill asks that the scene not be played in a plain natural way. The room should feel like a cage, and the men should look strong, stooped, and half trapped by their work.
the-haunters-the-haunted-ghost-stories-a: Ernest Rhys edited The Haunters & The Haunted. The book holds ghost stories and tales of the supernatural. Daniel O'Connor published it in London in 1921. Rhys also wrote the introduction. The contents list literary ghost stories. The first is The Fall of the House of Usher. Later titles include The Old Nurse's Story. The list also names The Haunted and the Haunters. What is present here stops with the front matter. The stories themselves do not appear.
the-last-hope: Henry Seton Merriman wrote a novel whose chapter titles trace kings, castaways, secrets, and gamblers across thirty-seven chapters. Only the title page and full contents are present here, naming early chapters such as Le Roi Est Mort, Vive Le Roi, and the return of the ship called the Last Hope. Later titles point to Gemosac, the Pont Royal, and a banker. The story itself does not appear in this record, so the contents alone sketch its French and maritime turns.
the-real-dope:
Ring W. Lardner lets baseball player Jack Keefe write home to his friend Al from a troop ship on January 15, in letters full of misspelling and slang. Keefe admits the letters cannot be mailed until the ship crosses, so Al will receive them all at once like a book.

Keefe promises the real dope seen with his own eyes, unlike newspaper reports written far from the front. The comedy comes from his confidence and his grammar alike, as ordinary shipboard life becomes war reporting. Readers get a famous comic voice applied to the First World War crossing.
the-shadow-of-the-rope: E. W. Hornung's The Shadow of the Rope is dated 1902 in its header. The edition shown is dated 1906 and illustrated by Harvey T. Dunn. Hornung dedicated it to his friend Edward Shortt. A single line of narrative precedes the title page. A woman had recoiled into a narrow hall, driven by uncontrollable revulsion, it says. The pages then give the contents, running to fourteen chapters. The end of their life and the case for the Crown open the list. Battle Royal closes the portion shown. No chapter text itself appears.
